issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, the trigger 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile clinically unless there is additional trauma content involving female perpetrators or a separate interpersonal trauma; nothing else in the profile supports that specific gendered trigger.

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: 'When people say things like my ex' implies a salient intimate-relationship trauma context that is not reflected anywhere else in the threat, memory, appraisal, or strategy items, making it a poor fit with the stated index trauma of terrorism.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after terrorism, but phrasing the event as happening 'because of the way I acted' suggests a strong personal-causation formulation. With the rest of the profile centered on external danger, startle, flashbacks, and monitoring others, this specific appraisal is insufficiently supported and sits awkwardly with the terrorism trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger item about 'my ex' is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of terrorism and the rest of the profile. It implies an intimate-relationship trauma context rather than reminders of a terrorist event, whereas the other trigger items (old photos, alcohol smell) and threat items are trauma-related.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the terrorism trauma context as presented here. In the absence of any terrorism-specific circumstance suggesting personal responsibility, 'The event happened because of the way I acted' implies causal responsibility for the attack, which is clinically implausible for this patient profile and not supported by the other selected items.

vignette:
Linh Tran is a 57-year-old Vietnamese American interior designer who has been married for nearly thirty years. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 72, seeking help for the first time following what she describes as a "breaking point" she can no longer manage alone.

Approximately two years ago, Linh was attending a design trade exposition at a convention center when a coordinated terrorist attack unfolded in the building. She was in a crowded exhibition hall when the first explosion occurred. In the chaos that followed, she was pressed against a display wall by the surging crowd, unable to move, surrounded by screaming and the acrid smell of smoke mixed with the spilled alcohol from a nearby hospitality bar that had been overturned in the stampede. She watched a man near her sustain a serious injury. She remained trapped in that corner for what she later learned was forty minutes before emergency personnel reached her. She was physically unharmed.

In the weeks after the attack, Linh found herself unable to look at the photographs she had taken at the exposition before the event occurred. She had loaded them onto her laptop intending to delete them, but the moment the thumbnails appeared on the screen, something shifted violently inside her - the hall, the heat, the noise - and she slammed the laptop shut. Since then, old photos of any kind, even family albums her husband leaves on the coffee table, have become difficult to be near. She has come to understand, in her own wordless way, that images carry the past too close to the surface. Similarly, the smell of alcohol - at dinner parties, in restaurants, even from her husband's occasional glass of wine - lands on her with a physical force she cannot explain to others. She has quietly stopped attending social events where drinking is likely, telling colleagues she is simply busy.

Talking about the attack remains impossible. When a close friend raised it gently over lunch eight months ago, Linh felt the room tilt. She excused herself, said she was fine, and has not had lunch with that friend since. In her work as an interior designer, client meetings occasionally involve discussing high-profile public venues - hotels, event spaces - and she has begun declining those commissions without explanation, a pattern that has started to cost her professionally and has left her business partner confused and quietly frustrated.

There are moments during the day when Linh is no longer in her studio but back inside the convention center - not remembering it, but inhabiting it, the crush of bodies, the smell. These episodes arrive without warning, and she has come to dread them as evidence that something in her mind has broken permanently. She has come to believe that she is simply not built to withstand ordinary difficulty anymore, that the slightest disruption - a delayed delivery, a disagreement with a client - undoes her entirely. When someone touches her shoulder unexpectedly, even her husband reaching for her in the kitchen, she startles so sharply that she has knocked things from countertops. She watches strangers in public with a quiet, exhausting vigilance, scanning for something she cannot name but is certain she would recognize. The world, she has concluded, is not safe and never was; she simply had not been paying close enough attention before.

To manage what she cannot articulate, Linh has developed a set of private rituals. She runs - far more than is healthy for her joints, which now ache chronically - because the physical effort quiets something. She eats in ways that comfort and distract her, often alone after her husband has gone to bed. And on the worst nights, she has hurt herself physically, pressing her nails into her forearm or striking her thigh, not from a wish to die but because the sharp sensation seems to interrupt the unbearable pressure building inside her. She has told no one about this.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was her husband finding her one evening on the kitchen floor, unable to explain why she was crying. She saw his face - frightened, helpless - and felt a shame she could not bear. She hopes, more than anything, that she is not beyond help. What she fears most is that she is.
